[h1] 先说结论：不推荐以现在的价格入手这个游戏 [/h1] 然后说说原因，本游戏采用回合制塔防的核心游戏方式，加入了经营和肉鸽的元素。类似之前的边境开拓者那个游戏。 游戏内没有关卡是类似传统塔防里的无尽模式，会根据不同的波次不断增加更困难的事件。 游戏内的经营元素是游戏中有一些资源，你需要每回合决策是把资源投入加强生产还是建造塔防。 游戏内的肉鸽元素是游戏内会给你一些随机增加防御塔的加强词条，还会掉落一些带有buff的装备，或者带有不同词条和法术的英雄。 传统游戏里的炮塔升级是进化出不同的分支类型，这种分支升级被游戏添加进了肉鸽词条中，玩家可以确定的固定升级就变成只能升级属性。 从游戏体验上来说，一开始上手这个游戏你会体验到游戏的平衡性问题，在前几次的游戏体验中你可能都很难会撑到第十波敌人的到来，后面即使升级了一些局内词条也仍然会感觉在对待敌人的时候有些力不从心，我游玩的还只是普通模式的难度。 [h3] 我觉得这个问题归结于一系列的问题上。 [/h3] 首先我认为游戏并没有展现肉鸽元素的精髓，随机词条引起的质变。不同稀有度的词条更像是同一个词条的升级版。目前的游玩中并没有遇到一些特别会引起游戏塔防的质变的【爽】词条。而肉鸽的一大魅力就是，如果随机到了很厉害的词条就会进入一段时间的割草模式。我认为制作组可能是不想要因为肉鸽导致游戏变得过于缺少策略性，但是目前的肉鸽元素和构建对我来说更像是普通的随机升级，而这种随机升级之间的间隔又足够长导致我并不期待它会给我带来什么。 关于炮塔部分，一些炮塔的属性介绍的不够明确，没有过多的介绍的情况下，玩家只能通过不断试错来选择使用什么炮塔搭配，例如游戏中一共有8种炮塔，箭塔（普通，单体，流血），石塔（范围燃烧），寒冰（范围冷冻），暗影（范围虚弱），渡鸦（单体，高额伤害）这几种炮塔可以用简单的词语形容出他们的作用，而激光炮塔，闪电炮塔，飓风炮塔之间的职责和类型则比较混淆不知道他们之间应该怎么选择。而且渡鸦比起一个单独炮塔，更像是箭塔的改版，它的作用和价格感觉并没办法匹配它的能力。 然后是关于敌人，作为一个塔防游戏，不能够方便的预测接下来会出现什么类型的敌人，敌人的能力是什么，应该用什么方式来针对后面的敌人，我觉得这是这个游戏难度比较大的原因之一，大多数的时候，你只能通过炮塔的组合和试错来看看应该大概怎么对付敌人，失败了就重新来。而不是可以在回合前观看敌人类型和数量来决定去使用什么炮塔。 关于经营部分，跟怪物的成长曲线相比，使用物资加大经营的决策的收益回报率不够高，这部分的物资数值不够宽容。很多物资的收益经营需要比较长的回报周期，而做出这种决策，很容易会被前面几波怪物干掉。这也跟观察不到敌人的数量和类型息息相关。你无法知道自己到底应该做出哪种决策才是更好的选择。 最后是美术部分，游戏整体风格采用比较省力和预算的low poly建模。对于敌人我除了他们身上的蓝和绿色血条之外基本看不出太多其他有辨识度的内容。 整体体验下来的感受就是，忙忙碌碌的玩了一会，做了一些决策，结果被两拨怪冲死了，玩家很难做出预防和有效的反制手段。[b] 感觉制作组花费了大量时间考虑经营和塔防还有肉鸽之间的互动设计，但是没有花费太多的时间考虑敌人和塔防之间的设计，或者说敌人带给玩家的体验。 [/b] 我不排斥一个游戏可以硬核和高难度，但对于一款商业游戏而言，我觉得让玩家起码不在前面几个小时被劝退也是一个很重要的部分。 所以综上所述这些体验结合，我认为这个游戏并没有符合目前它的售价设定，如果游戏在30-50元，可能会是一个更合理的入手区间。 如果你耐心的看完了整篇内容，并且觉得这些点和价格的组合对你来说都不是问题，那么请直接购买，这些仅仅作为个人意见，仅供参考。

1. 随机性太弱，目前的buff内容和机制导致几乎不可能遇到常规肉鸽中一波肥的爽局，是否存在这种能爽的buff构筑也持怀疑态度，轻度肉鸽的核心难道是轻度？ 2. 难度曲线不合理，为了避免前十关暴毙，发育构筑套路限制很大，自由发挥空间小。思维完全被难度曲线固化了，发散思维、尝试多种策略往往意味着花样暴毙，正反馈、参与感都大大降低了。 3. 美工一言难尽，除了蓝绿血条和boss血条旁的白色符号外，怪物完全没有记忆点与区分度；基地发育部分也没有常规经营游戏的深度与趣味性，城市管理与塔防构筑间的配合联动太过僵硬，硬拼在一起的感觉。 目前的游戏状态不推荐入手，玩玩demo就够了。

Very misleading description and trailer. This game has no city building and has an incredibly uninspired basic economy balance even for a tower defence game. Lacking depth, content and balance is incredibly shameful for a rogue-lite session-based tower-defense game: - Every run feels exactly the same thanks to lacking enemy variety and low amount of content overall - no regions, no player choice, no interesting challenges or "easter eggs". - Your build and synergies are mostly decided by RNG rolls for upgrades, and not by your "idea" or "plan" to cook up some interesting combo or interaction. Even then they feel basic aside from a few rare *unique* upgrades that are a half-step above the usual DPS increase. - Over-reliance on meta unlocks to pan out play time. Basically a lot of mechanics and upgrades are barred behind meta currency that is almost directly tied to time spent in-game. You cant expect to finish runs without clocking up currency to allow you to become powerful enough to beat scaled up waves even if your build is onpoint and your theorycrafting checks out. - No city building, no city planning. Its just an upgrade tree in the form of a few different buildings that boost your resource gain for building or upgrading towers. Another thing worth mentioning is that it uses free low poly asset packs that are sometimes incredibly clashing, ruining any semblance of an art style, hero portraits especially. Overall, cant recommend it.
8分。 一路玩下去，从各种细节上能各感受到制作组的用心，是真正热爱游戏的人才能做出来的。 从游戏性上，是满分的。 -0.5分，美术上还是差点意思，并非是建模和美术风格的问题，而就是，差点意思。 -1.5分，你这个定价未免太贵了，高出市面上同种类型的游戏的定价，你的美术也让我觉得不值这个价钱。 总之，推荐入，但在五折前不推荐入。

This is [u]not[/u] the best tower defense game you will ever play. However, it is doing some things that make it worth considering. There are things I like about this game and some things I really do not like. Weigh them for yourself and make your own judgment call. [b]Meta Progress[/b] A lot of people like this feature - but 90% of the meta progression in this game is straight power creep or options that you really need if you want to build a successful run. I really dislike games that gate your ability to beat the game behind meta progression and this game commits that sin in pretty egregious ways. You would do well to beat the first boss in this game without meta progression, much less see the game through all the waves. For me, that is a really frustrating experience and for others, it is a feature. Judge for yourself. [b]Tower Diversity[/b] There are only 8 towers, which is fine. Their upgrade options by leveling are pretty generic. The game turns itself into a roguelike through the "Banner" system and "Relic" system that supports it. The relic system is what you would expect from any roguelike and the system is just average. Not terrible, but not exceptional either. The banners are where the game is supposed to really open up and there are some interesting ideas here. Certain towers can get upgrades/synergies if you get the correct banner combinations together encouraging you to experiment with towers that work together. This is probably the only space in the game that encourages replayability and while the system is interesting, it was not compelling enough to carry the whole game for me. [b]Replayability[/b] The game has no variation whatsoever in the enemy compositions. The map will expand and change in a procedurally generated fashion, but that doesn't change too much about how you are going to attack the game. You know you have to meet a certain DPS gate for each wave, and that DPS gate isn't going to change because the units pushing you never change from run to run. All replayability is pushed on the shoulders of the banner and relic system - and while those systems are fine or even good, they can't carry the entire game. [b]Conclusion[/b] So - if you've read this far it seems pretty strange that I am still recommending this game. This is not the best tower defense game ever built, but it doesn't have to be. For the price point, the game is fair and it is appealing to people that have different tastes than me. That is fine and I think it is a really high quality mobile game sitting on PC and serving a group that enjoys these kind of systems. I'll probably come back and pick at this one every now and then, but it definitely is a "meh" for my personal tastes.

这游戏不错，差评是我需要给制作组提点建议。 如果肉鸽元素不体现在经济发展上，那么每局游戏的运营思路就会非常相似，甚至可以有一个公式化的最优解。 同时造的塔越多，旗帜强化的选择也就越多，也就是所谓的卡池污染越严重，这就背离了塔防游戏打配合的核心策略。 建议：1增加经济方面的随机性奖励，鼓励玩家着重发展某种资源 2增加随机奖励的次数，最好每个回合都给玩家一次抉择机会，奖励可以把多种塔的增强叠加，比如ABC三种旗帜，A加强箭塔和闪电塔，B加强减速和激光塔，C加强投石和闪电塔这样。

Since I’ve put some more hours into Nordhold, I thought it was time to rewrite my review—though I’m still leaving it negative for now. Let’s start with the positives: Nordhold is a roguelite tower defense game featuring procedurally generated maps, unlockable power-ups for future runs, a banner system for run-specific bonuses, and an endless mode. The procedural map generation keeps each run feeling fresh, and the banner system is well-designed, offering strategic variety. There are dozens of banners, rewarding both broad tower setups and focused builds. For about 30 hours, the game delivered a solid experience. I unlocked all the power-ups and cleared wave 30, which marks the end of the standard mode. Since then, I’ve been stuck trying to beat wave 37—a major difficulty spike. And that’s the core issue: beyond that point, there's little meaningful content. At €20, 30–40 hours of gameplay might feel short, especially when progression hits a near-impossible wall. I enjoy endless roguelites and I don’t mind a challenge when progressing beyond the intended game length (I’m playing Balatro too), but this difficulty jump feels less like a curve and more like a brick wall. Another issue is RNG—both in map layout and banners. While you can reroll and influence banners, your success heavily depends on getting the right ones. Banners come in common, rare, and legendary tiers, and getting the a lot of bad or the wrong ones can cripple your strategy. In other roguelites like Hades the choice of a bad boon is mitigated, because your skill can carry you. In Nordhold, your influence is mostly limited to tower placement and a few spells, so bad luck hurts more. Finally, there are two stronger starting bonuses you can unlock, each with a drawback. One gives more starting resources but buffs enemies, while the other offers a high-tier relic, though you can’t undo the choice once made. These options are only available if you reached wave 10 in your previous run. While not essential, it’s frustrating to be locked out of all enhanced starts when the only thing left for me is to beat is wave 37—forcing unnecessary grinding just to attempt it with all options available.

Meta progress doesn't stack your power, it's basically just core features walled behind the "too long tutorial" (8h spend didnt unlock all the core features still). Tower defence part is fine until you realise there is actually not that much variations that actually work (especially on higher ascendance), and base/eco building is basically spamming the same order in every game because starting bonuses doesn't affect that at all (maybe a little, but still same order). Upd.: Well, they released a couple of major updates, adding meta-progression tree and some balance changes. Which is good in general but unfortunately it is still just not fun to play.

By Odin’s beard, Nordhold is a stormborn saga of steel, blood, and unyielding glory! If you’ve ever dreamed of commanding the walls of Asgard itself against the wrath of Hel’s minions, this is your shieldwall to stand behind! This isn’t your grandmother’s tower defense – this is a roguelike honour-hunt through the Nine Realms, where every defeat teaches, and every victory is a feast worthy of Einherjar. Every run is a saga anew, as we amass honour across battles and unlock upgrades that feel like blessings from Freyja herself. You'll craft synergies stronger than Urd’s own threads, weaving death upon your foes with runestones, archers, and the fury of frost and flame. The visuals sing like skalds by the hearthfire – every map a windswept fjord or cursed ruin, steeped in myth and mystery. The music? By the Norns, it stirs the soul like war drums echoing across the Bifröst! As eternal as Yggdrasil’s roots, as eternal is the replayability of this game. With procedurally generated maps, upgrades chosen like fates cast by the Norns, and difficulty that rises like the Midgard Serpent, Nordhold begs to be played again and again. You will fall – but like a true Norse warrior, you’ll rise stronger, smarter, more savage. 10/10 – Would die gloriously on wave 42 and scream “FOR VALHALLA!” while restarting.

In its core, I think Nordhold is a competent TD game. But I severely dislike the early game (which you play a lot because it's a rogue-lite), especially the base management part and slow tower upgrade progression. It is always the same the first few waves, you always reroll until you get one certain buff in the start (if you allow free rerolls, you should just remove that choice altogether). And then you upgrade the same buildings the same way every time. And you place the same basic towers aswell, until your economy allows otherwise. It's just a chore (especially with Steam Deck controls) with no real strategic decisions. That changes in Midgame though, so if you can tolerate the repeating early part, the base management adds some strategic depth later on. And for sure there a some nice tower synergies, if you survive long enough to build them. I can't judge difficulty - i didn't get that far, but i also didn't unlock everything yet. But i also don't have interest in doing so anymore. If you're a genre fan, i would still recommend to at least try this game. But for me it's too tedious to play for any longer.

You know ... this game would really work well if it weren't a rogue-lite. That single fact takes it from a game in which you could expand continuously with an economy behind you to a very uninspired low-economy snooze fest in the first 20 or so waves ... What I mean by that is that even with some upgrades to get more starting resources, the game is just SOOOOO slow to get started, but then ramps up the difficulty immensely fast, which somehow means I can now often not even get past the first boss for some reason, whereas I had already reached the 3rd or 4th one, even with better upgrades, which leaves only one real conclusion: the game is entirely dependant on RNG. And the base management is just tedious. A simple QoL change alone would move your cursor to your base when a defensive round is over ... instead of having to slowly scroll there. Placing towers is where the RNG is the most egregious. Since you never know HOW a map gets expanded (in which direction), a tower can either be placed in a really good or a really bad spot, and you need the really good spots, since towers get exponentially more expensive the more you place, so if they don't have overlapping fields to soften the enemy up beforehand, then you're ♥♥♥♥ out of luck ... and I've been ♥♥♥♥ out of luck for a long time now, meaning the enemies just walk down a very long path until they get to my last line of defense, which they quickly overwhelm then. Upgrading your towers either feels impactful (like doubling the range) or meaningless (like increasing the attack rate from 0.1 to 0.11 lol, wtf?). So some upgrades are just useless. I don't know how the tower fusions really work, either, but I'm only missing 2 more towers to unlock, and man this is a grind I'm not sure I can stomach anymore. Either you're wasting resources on towers you actually don't even need, like arrow towers for the most part seem entirely pointless after the first few waves, unless I'm missing something and they turn into high powered gatling cannons later on, while Lightning Towers seem absolutely essential to even make a dent in the enemy waves. They're the only reliable source of AOE damage it seems, whereas the beam towers are the only reliable source of ramping up single target damage somehow. The music and presentation is also not very good. It's the same basic "ohdhodhod" track that's playing constantly. It's kinda grating. Visually the game isn't much to look at. Like I said, the game could have been great as a sort of campaign ... get stronger to keep up with the enemies from "map" to "map", instead of resetting your progress to 0 with every start ... here I am, waiting for my ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ wheat and wood to come in to get more workers to increase my income yet again, while being steamrolled by the enemy. Edit: After some testing my opinion is unchanged. After level 20 at the latest (if the game has been "nice" to you up to that point), enemy scaling just goes through the roof, and you go from "hey, I can do this" to "oh god, 100 enemies just rammed into my castle gate". Likewise, the micro management just gets increasingly annoying. Wheat basically becomes useless, because the passive generation seems to be enough to keep the beer flowing for the production bonus. Towers, however, get so expensive that you will never keep up, no matter how many resources you produce. Not to mention that some towers become worse later in the game when you build new ones, like the Lightning Tower that can get stronger the longer it exists (through additive crit rate). You basically have to invest a lot of gold to increase their crit chance from 10% to like at least 75%, so gold becomes the most important factor, but then you're micro managing all your towers again, having almost no overview what level they are. You have so many towers later on, it's just ... tedious.

I am a BIG fan of strategic Tower Defense games. And Nordhold delivers the fun in spades. I've played for 132 hours, and for me, the replayability still strongly compels me for 'just one more game.' Each turn a new random tile is laid out to extend the path. Every third turn, YOU get to choose one of three tiles to place down. So the layout can vary from game to game, and you actually have some agency in how it lays out. Things that Nordhold has that bumps the gameplay up another notch: 1) The nine tower types each feel unique with their own qualities involving both tactical and strategic implementation. 2) Banners can be acquired that can grant unique qualities to ALL towers of that same type. And then those qualities can be further augmented with further banners! One banner for the electric towers even grants an ability for individual electric towers to further level up just by scoring critical hits! 3) Towers can synergize with each other depending on your choices and playstyle. There are even special banners to further amplify certain synergies. 4) Relics can alter gameplay or even enhance towers. Relics can be obtained by quests, killing bosses/elites, or via the market. These are some of my favorite features, but there are even more... THINGS THAT NEED IMPROVEMENT (in my opinion) 1) While the village has an impact on how the game unfolds, i find village management to often be tedious. a) making an adjustment to a village building scrolls you off the battlefield and over to the building. You then have to manually scroll back to the battlefield for tower placement or play. b) village buildings are too far apart (I'm looking at YOU, LIGHT HOUSE.) Scrolling around to check on stuff is Tedious. In fact, all village management could be condensed into a single screen where everything is presented at a single glance. The village impacts play, but how it's implemented is a downer to me. c) when i mouse over a tower on the build menu, there is no tool tip showing me its stats. If it's the first one im building, i find out AFTER i place it. If I have built prior ones of that type, i have to go find it and select it to show me its current stats. d) I have yet to find an in game tutorial or even a glossary of enemy unit types and abilities. After 100 hours in game, I'm still finding out stuff that I didn't know I could do. OVERALL: The cool stuff far over shadows my personal nit picks. If you enjoy tower defense games, then I recommend you give it a go, even at full price. On sale, it's a steal!

My recommendation for Nordhold is about 80% yes, because there are some important caveats. Nordhold is a fairly fun rogue-lite tower defense game with a heavy emphasis on resource management. Each wave, you increase the path length by adding one large hex field onto the path, which opens up new areas to place towers, branching pathways that split the enemy's spawn locations, or other map features. There are nine towers at this time, from a long range Volcano Mortar, the short range melty beam Runestone, and my personal favorite chain-attacking Arc towers. The most prominent feature in front of you on your Tower Defense map will be the topography range bonuses. When you have selected a tower to place, you will see some hex tiles with a number, from 1-4. Each number increases the range of the tower by a flat 0.5 hexes. For the Volcano Mortars, this is a fairly small improvement to their large base range, but is a massive improvement to short range towers like the Runestone or Frost towers. These topography range bonuses mark out the best spots to place towers, or to maximize their distance. There are also other buff hexes, the one I see almost exclusively being the range hexes that increase a tower's range by a percentage. These hexes still gain the topography flat bonuses. Other buff hexes I've seen include a 50% damage increase, and automatically giving your tower 250% barrier damage. There is a lot of fun in building up your tower placement and strategy within a run, as the Banner system asks you to focus on certain weapons in your arsenal. However, there is a bit of a problem with the structure of the setup: your options for improving your defenses is greatly outmatched by the enemy creeps' scaling. At base, a tower has improvement costs starting at 15 gold, which is a pretty hefty ask at the beginning of a run. For each wave a specific tower is on the map, that number decreases by 5. So older towers will eventually receive free buffs. Each time a tower is upgraded, the price resets to 15 gold +5 for each time that tower has had its level increased. There are a few abilities or upgrades that speed this process up, but generally it means that a level 4 tower needs 30 gold to upgrade. Now, each upgrade to towers is fairly small. The core stats are damage, range, and fire rate, with each upgrade increasing these stats by 20% of their base value (arrow towers base damage is 110, each damage upgrade increases their damage by 22, etc). The other stats are crit chance, crit damage, accuracy, penetration, and barrier damage. these are always upgraded the same amount regardless of the tower. These upgrades are 10% for crit chance, 40% crit damage (all towers have base 180% crit damage), 25% accuracy and penetration, and 100% barrier damage. Accuracy cuts through Block, which is a chance for an enemy creep to ignore an attack, Penetration ignores a percentage of an enemies armor, which reduces the damage the enemy takes by a percentage, and barriers are special enemies that have a bubble shield that absorbs all damage that enemies within the bubble would take. The barrier breaks when the barrier enemy dies, or the barrier's health bar is depleted. Barrier damage is a multiplier of the tower's attack affects a barrier health bar. The exact numbers of Block and Armor are not explained very well, and are absolutely miniscule icons above an individual creep's health bar. That's a lot to say about tower upgrades, and remember these are either happening infrequently (once every 3+ waves) or cost large amounts of gold (depending on the age of the tower). The first wave is basically 3 100 health creeps, and wave 10 will have a boss with 3k hp and dozens of 2-500 hp creeps. The enemies scale very fast, but your towers don't. It means that no individual tower is all that good, it is instead a numbers game: do I have enough towers to chunk down these waves over the length of the track? However, each tower you build increases the cost of that tower class, meaning you will quickly price yourself out of building another Arc Tower if you only build Arc Towers. However, banners encourage you to use a specific category of tower, meaning... The enemies' scaling demands having as many towers as possible, the cost of towers incentivizes diversifying your tower choice to keep your build prices reasonable, upgrading individual towers requires extreme resource generation or time that you don't have, and the banner system wants you to narrow in on a specific class of tower. These systems are pulling you in different directions, which can feel terrible if you simply aren't lucky. Additionally, the towers are not particularly balanced. Shadow Towers have decent damage, average range, the 2nd best attack speed, fire multiple projectiles, and apply the weakness debuff which increases the damage enemies take. It's quite expensive, so it probably wouldn't be your first tower, but you can generally see the effects of Shadow Towers immediately. Tornado Towers place a tornado on the enemy track that deals damage to all creeps that it passes over. However, it deals slightly more damage than a single projectile of Shadow towers, is lower range, lower attack rate, and has no inherent debuff. Tornado tower banners also feel pretty terrible. They can receive a stun effect, but even the legendary variant of this ability only lasts 0.7 seconds, and then the enemy cannot be stunned by another tornado tower for 10 seconds. Unless you have a godlike layout for slowing effects and your tornado tower's placement, a single Tornado tower will never stun the same enemy twice. They can receive a percentage increase to their (very low) damage based on the missing health of an enemy. Tornado towers are very good early, as they are good against low-health enemies and help when you get to later creeps that spawn superfast low-health enemies. However, there's no world where you can build around tornado towers. They simply don't have the base stats or upgrades to make that feel possible. Fusion banners are acquired if you have 3 banners of two different towers, and those tower classes have a fusion category. Arc Towers and Tornado Towers don't have a Fusion, so they simply don't work together. Each fusion has 2 options, and they are occasionally awful. For example, one of the fusions for Arrow+Arc is that Arc tower chain attacks will spread the Arrow tower's bleed debuff. That's pretty cool... Except if you don't have a banner giving your Arrow towers the bleed debuff. Some fusions are based on getting specific banners, and those fusions are useless if you didn't happen to get offered the banner in question. One last small gripe I have with the game is how it is unkind with stacking upgrades. If you have a buff that gives a tower a 10% damage increase, that will not effect the flat value increases from upgrading individual towers. +10% dmg Arrow towers deal 121 damage, but the upgrades are still 22 instead of 24. However, [i] Percentage decreases to stats will reduce the flat values you receive. [/i] So if you get the banner for Arrows that decrease their damage to, let's say 50%, but fires in 3 shot bursts, the flat damage increase of upgrades will instead be 11. Percentage increases are applied exclusively to the base damage, but percentage decreases are applied universally across the tower. It's a very mean-spirited calculation. Ultimately, the game is quite fun if you like tower defense games and resource management. While the tower diversity and unique upgrades are nice, they conflict with the scaling of the enemies and how building up your defense works. Some runs are simply doomed from the word go because you don't get high rarity or high quality banners, good hero abilities, viable relics, workable tower hexes, or favorable paths. I would still recommend it, as it's a pretty good game to chill out over, but I don't think you need to go out of your way to play it.

The grahics, roguelikes upgrades and the map are all positives. The minus is the actual tower defense, its a classic system of walking the line between defending the coming waves while also not over investing in defenses. You need to build your economic engine without dying while doing so, the issue comes from the fact that its extremely hard to know what defenses or how many of them you need. Walking the line is really hard when you get 0 information to go on. Usually what happened to me was, "its easy, its easy, its easy, ouch I'm dead". A painful experience after investing 30 minutes or more of solid engine building. Obviously I made a mistake but the issue is there really was no way for me to discern the increase in difficulty beforehand. The biggest issue however is the endgame, the final 10 waves of the 30 waves normal game. They get insane and you need very particular strategies to succeed, which sucks the fun out of a "choose your own strategy" kind of game. The late game has tons of enemies, some of them have huge magic shield protecting the weaker enemies under it, others have armor that reduces damage, others have dodges which makes all shots likely to miss and do 0 damage. Others are tanks that becomes a horde when they die, others have healing auras, meaning they heal all the small enemies around them. So if you almost kill all the enemies but there is a small break until your next set of towers, you die. Others have immunity to 2 or more hits, they will never take damage from first 2 attacks. The combination of all the above level of ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ means you need very specific strategy, you need a killzone, otherwise healers or tank spawners are going to kill you. You need aoe to kill all the hordes, you need single target damage very high for the shielders, tanks bosses and so on. You need magic barrier kill strategy, you also need a way to get around dodge and immunity. The game tells you none of these things before they hit you in the face with them or even while they are hitting you. It just doesn't feel good to play the tower defense part, which is the majority of the game. Endgame updating and spending your resources also becomes a drag

Note: This was written during season 4 and forgotten on my computer. I have not played season 5, so some issues were hopfully resolved. TLDR: Nordhold is a fun game for a while, but once most things are unlocked, The economy side of things can feel repetitive. Pushing to higher waves(past the final boss) seems like it requires good RNG and certain tower builds. Starting with the good: On the surface, the loop sounds nice. A rougelite tower defense game where you gradually get stronger to push further along the game. Unlock towers and perks to get more powerful and get further to unlock even more things. Each run will be unique as the map is generated gradually during each wave and you start with a different relic/bonus. There is the usual variety of towers that are common in tower defense games such as the basic arrow tower, the cold tower, the long range mortar tower, the sniper tower, and the close range beam tower. These towers will slowly get stronger by leveling up where you can power up one of their characteristics such as range or damage. Additionally, there are perks(called banners) which will further strengthen one type of tower, usually in somewhat unique ways such as splitting attacks into multiple but weaker ones. Picking only a single tower’s banners will eventually unlock an ultimate skill which can significantly strengthen them. Otherwise, there is a fusion system where choosing banners of two compatible towers will let you pick between two synergistic skills. To build towers, there is an economic system with resources such as wood, stone, wheat, and gold. Wood is used to build most buildings, outposts, and some towers. Stone is used for more advanced towers. Wheat is used to hire villagers and brew beer. Gold is used to buy building upgrades, tower upgrades, and relics. Other buildings have functions such as healing your life total, researching tech, or increasing productivity. So there are choices that have to be made between strengthening your defense or economy/tech. In the beginning, you don’t have every option unlocked. You need to gradually unlock towers and city buildings.There are also meta upgrades that provide you permanent bonuses such as an increased worker or more starting resources. You won’t need all of of them to finish the game for the first time and it does give you some feeling of progression. After unlocking all the meta upgrades, winning to the final boss isn’t too difficult. Then you can move to the additional waves. This is where things take a hard turn. Level 38 is the bane of many runs where a sudden jump in difficulty causes the run to end where the previous levels never even got close. If you have good RNG and strategy, it is doable, but expect most builds not to have enough power to get through. There is a certain RNG element required to get into the higher levels, but the game does try to mitigate them somewhat. The map expands after every round, but with an upgrade, you can choose how the path expands every 3 rounds. You get a few choices for the bonus perk and starting bonus, but some are clearly more powerful than others. Banner choices are random as well, but this can be partially mitigated through research to increase rerolls or remove weaker options. Tower targeting can be prioritized with up to 3 priorities. These different priorities can range from distance, monster traits, or health. There is a further meta mode for additional grinding. Every run you can earn a bit of currency and unlock bonuses used in this mode. There are a lot of levels to unlock, so you can keep getting more powerful and push further waves. I played a few runs, but felt the currency earning rate was a bit slow. Overall, while the game is fun, I think there are currently limitations with build order. Once you know the minimum amount of towers needed to defend, you know the level of greed you can get away with. Thus a lot of the game can feel a bit samey. Of course the build order slightly changes depending on what towers you want to focus on. And the map changes every run, so towers need to be placed differently, but the strategy overall is the same.

When i saw this game release strongly describing and weighting how early they were in the development process I saw it like a train station with healthy tracks heading in varied directions where you could see great things on the horizon of all of them. I took their wording and tone to mean they were going to build destinations, but the game is the tracks it was at release. I ran it but i wouldn't ever say i played it, it just was never very fun. I put this off because I could see how it should have been. Primarily the big issues are, there is no important or non reflexive decision choice point or strategy to the map. You make the map, build a choke and try to keep your loop backs in range of your loop backs; your lucky and it works or not the end. Inflexibility in design leading to permanent tower placement and locked in skill choices. Once set you would be penalizing yourself to adjust or change. So there is simply no importance to your input after you have set the ball rolling after the first 5% of the match. The town is mono tone too simple a chore and a anchor. There is nothing new there from match to match, nothing to discover, and all you are doing in essence is choosing the level of risk you take on for reward. Conserve resources for gains risk losing. The resources you maximize are going to be the ones you are using, and your are simply going to get them, all the upgrades are good and you are going to get them in the optimal order, so all that is left is how long are you going to save your gold before buying what you have no choice but to buy. The roguelike features are in the form they are in a wild detriment to the game more than a boon. They make the start of the game feel terrible, the middle polka dotty, and the end monotone and stretched to infinity and beyond. I like roguelike progressive features, but these are simply put not any good and standing in the way of balance. Which brings me to the last. I have watched their patches and they are progressively slowing and were absolutely tiny to begin with. Nothing I view as a primary system has been added to the game, and given that updates are down to about 10% the content of the first 3 months it is safe to say the game is what it is intended to be at this point. TLDR: Disappointment aside, this is not a terrible tower defense game, but it is the kind of game that used to come out for free on flash sites and mid list in the tower defense section. It is what you see with no depth and all the hidden mystery in their marketing language referring to what it is or will be is vapor, nothing more.

There's definitely some enjoyment to be had with this title, but the balancing and progression is just so poorly executed. The roguelike aspects are in opposition with the consistent level of difficulty you will face in the early phases of the game - you have to draw the exact pieces you need to make whichever strategy you're trying, and even then it may come down to a dice roll on one of your tower's abilities triggering when you need it to, or the enemy path building out in a way that is optimal for your tower placement. On the other hand, once you cross a certain threshold in the run, it is effectively easy mode, because the only way to make it there is to have had everything work out in your favor up to that point. Most infuriatingly, you'll find most of the village buildings and abilities are not available to you until you have played quite a bit. The decisions on which buildings unlock early and which unlock late are sometimes cruel, especially in the case of the Druid House, which can heal your village shield (basically your health for when minions manage to make it through the gauntlet). Even that feature isn't amazingly helpful but, hey, doesn't that sound like something a newer player would take advantage of? It just all feels like a game that's designed to be overly difficult solely for the purpose of being overly difficult. Which, hey, it's gonna be someone's favorite game. Not mine, though. And probably not yours.
